meta.case_name: Rental Cars and Frequent Flyer Program

prompt.context: Our client is a US airline with a popular frequent flyer mile program. They sell frequent flyer miles through partnerships with credit card companies, hotels, and rental car agencies. While the business overall has been healthy, they have noticed a sharp decline in their frequent flyer miles revenue from the rental car segment: a 50% drop in the last two years.
prompt.question: Determine the cause for this loss in revenue from the rental car segment, and what the airline can do to reverse the trend.

clarifying_info.q: How long has the frequent flyer program been in place?
clarifying_info.a: Over 20 years. It was created for competitive advantage and customer retention. The client was among the first to implement such a program, but now almost every airline has one.

clarifying_info.q: How do car rental agencies sell these miles?
clarifying_info.a: An agency advertises that customers get X frequent flyer miles per rental day. When customers request the miles, they receive them and the agency pays the airline for the transaction.

clarifying_info.q: How many rental car agency partners does the client have?
clarifying_info.a: There are 7 major car rental agencies in the country. 5 of the 7 are partners with our client, and these 5 agencies comprise 97% of all rental car business in the US.

clarifying_info.q: Has the volume of car rentals changed?
clarifying_info.a: Number of cars rented has not gone down, and days per rental have not gone down.

clarifying_info.q: Do frequent flyer members prefer renting from partner agencies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — it is fair to assume that frequent flyer members would strongly prefer to rent a car that came with miles compared to one that did not.

framework: Understand the revenue structure: revenue = (miles sold per transaction) x (price per mile) x (number of transactions)
Identify which driver(s) have declined: volume of rentals, price per mile, or miles offered per rental
Explore the rental agency side: cost pressures, negotiation dynamics, competitive landscape
Assess solutions: pricing changes, exclusivity/partnership restructuring, mandate on minimum miles offered
Quantify value of proposed solution (exclusive partnership model) for both parties
Consider implementation risks and other strategic considerations

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the 50% revenue decline from rental car agencies?
questions.guidance: Volume (number of rentals, days per rental) has not changed. Price per mile was not lowered. The root cause is that rental agencies, seeking to lower costs, asked the airline to reduce the price per mile. When the airline refused, the agencies responded by offering fewer miles per rental day — reducing the volume of miles sold per transaction, which drove revenue down.

questions.prompt: Structure and solve the math to determine the rental agencies' willingness to pay (WTP) for an exclusive (semi-exclusive, 3-partner) arrangement, and estimate how much additional revenue the airline could capture.
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish variable vs. fixed costs. Marginal profit from extra rentals should use variable costs only. For simplicity, assume all fleet costs are variable. Key steps: (1) calculate current profit per agency, (2) calculate profit per agency under 3-partner model, (3) derive incremental WTP, (4) compare total WTP old vs. new.

math.setup: Assumptions: 10M rentals/year by frequent flyer members; $45/day average car rental; 3 days average rental; 10% margin for rental agencies before paying frequent flyer miles; currently 5 partners; propose cutting to 3 partners; current payment to airline is $3 per transaction.
steps: Profit per rental before FF miles: 10% x $135 = $13.50
Profit per rental after FF miles: $13.50 - $3.00 = $10.50
Total current profit per agency: $10.50 x 2M = $21M (equivalently: $27M gross profit minus $6M FF fees)
Gross profit per agency (3-partner): 10% x $135 x 3.33M = $45M
WTP for FF miles per agency (new): $45M - $21M = $24M (i.e., agency would pay up to $24M to maintain its same net profit as today)
Incremental WTP vs. current payment: $24M - $6M = $18M per agency
Incremental total revenue potential to airline: $72M - $30M = $42M
math.answer: The exclusive 3-partner arrangement could generate up to $42M in additional revenue for the airline. Even capturing half (~$21M) would represent a ~67% increase in revenue from rental car agencies.

questions.prompt: What considerations should be made when restructuring the partnership model with rental car agencies?
questions.guidance: This is a conversational brainstorming question. Strong answers cover: (1) how to select the 3 partners (auction, geographic coverage, customer preference survey, current market share among FF members); (2) whether customer loyalty to specific rental agencies could reduce total rental volume under exclusivity; (3) actual fixed vs. variable cost structure for agencies; (4) pricing mechanism (higher price per mile vs. mandated minimum miles per rental day); (5) whether a similar exclusive model could be applied to hotels.

brainstorming.prompt: What considerations would need to be made when restructuring the way the airline currently partners with rental car companies?

categories.name: Partner selection criteria
ideas: Survey frequent flyer customers for rental agency preference
Use current market-share data among frequent flyer members

categories.name: Customer behavior risks
ideas: Customers may have loyalty to specific rental agencies not chosen as partners, reducing total rentals
Total frequent flyer rental volume could shrink under an exclusive arrangement

categories.name: Cost structure clarity
ideas: Actual fixed vs. variable cost split for rental agencies needs verification — assuming all costs variable may underestimate the profit impact of the FF program

categories.name: Pricing mechanism
ideas: Price the new partnership via a higher price per mile
Mandate that exclusive partners offer a minimum number of FF miles per rental day

categories.name: Expansion opportunities
ideas: Apply the same exclusive-partnership logic to hotel partnerships if it is profitable in rental cars

recommendation: The 50% revenue decline is driven by rental agencies offering fewer miles per rental day after the airline refused to lower its per-mile price; volume of rentals has remained flat.

Recommend restructuring from 5 non-exclusive partners to 3 semi-exclusive partners. This reallocates frequent flyer customer volume across fewer agencies, raising each agency's WTP from $6M to $24M and increasing the airline's total addressable revenue from this segment by up to $42M — a potential 67% revenue gain even if only half is captured.
risks: Customer loyalty to excluded agencies could reduce total rental volume and erode projected gains
Fixed cost assumptions for agencies may be incorrect, affecting actual WTP calculations
Excluded agencies may seek partnerships with competing airlines, weakening the exclusive value proposition
Transition and renegotiation complexity could create short-term revenue disruption
next_steps: Survey frequent flyer members on rental agency preferences to inform partner selection
Obtain more granular cost data from agencies to refine WTP estimates
Design auction or RFP process to select the 3 exclusive partners
Evaluate feasibility of applying a similar exclusive model to hotel partnerships
